title: Cable-TV frequency division: many DRAM dies share one RF line
idea: Adapted from DOCSIS cable-TV plant: each DRAM die on a stack or interposer gets its own RF carrier (e.g., eight carriers spread over 10-80 GHz) on one shared transmission line, using tiny on-die mixers instead of dedicated wires. Dies tune in and out like set-top boxes on a multi-drop coax-like trace.
why: Attacks interposer/TSV wiring tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): ~4-8x fewer wires per GB/s and more dies per channel for capacity, targeting <1 pJ/bit at short reach.

title: Fiber-to-the-home splitter broadcasts model weights to many accelerators
idea: Adapted from passive optical networks (PON): a shared weight-memory pool transmits each layer's weights once on an optical channel, and a passive 1:32 splitter delivers the same stream to 32 accelerators at the same moment. Each accelerator keeps only KV-cache and activations in local HBM, not its own copy of the weights.
why: Replicated weights across data/pipeline-parallel GPUs waste scarce HBM; broadcast removes up to Nx duplication (30-60% of HBM freed per GPU) and replaces N reads with one.

title: Video-codec P-frames for tensors: ship only deltas between tiles
idea: Adapted from MPEG motion-compensated inter-frame coding: the controller and a logic layer in the DRAM base die keep a reference tile and send only quantized residuals for activation, KV or optimizer tiles that change little step to step. Periodic 'I-frames' bound drift.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth (fact 5): temporally correlated AI tensors could need 2-4x fewer bits on the bus, multiplying effective HBM bandwidth and capacity.

title: Deep-space LDPC coding lets memory links run at 50 mV swing
idea: Adapted from deep-space probes that trade coding gain for transmit power: the DRAM bus carries a short high-rate LDPC/polar code so swing drops from ~250-400 mV to ~50 mV. The PHY decoder cleans a raw BER of 1e-4 down to 1e-18.
why: I/O pJ/bit and CV^2 floor (facts 5, 10): link energy scales ~V^2, so 5x lower swing could cut I/O energy 3-10x net of decoder cost.

title: Radar phased-array beams link compute boards to remote memory sleds
idea: Adapted from military AESA radar tiles: 60-140 GHz beam-steered phased arrays on memory sleds and compute boards form reconfigurable wireless links across a rack. Any accelerator can steer a beam to any memory sled without cables or connectors.
why: Disaggregation recovers stranded DRAM (often 25-50% idle per server) and removes cabling cost; target ~5 pJ/bit at 100 Gb/s per beam.

title: Telecom MEMS optical cross-connects time-share memory pools among accelerators
idea: Adapted from MEMS-mirror optical circuit switches in telecom cores: fiber links between memory shelves and accelerators are re-pointed in milliseconds, moving terabytes of DRAM to whichever job is in its memory-heavy phase (e.g., decode versus prefill).
why: Raises usable supply by cutting overprovisioning; circuit-switched light adds no per-bit switching energy; ~20-40% less DRAM per cluster.

title: Endoscope imaging bundles carry microLED arrays for off-package HBM bandwidth
idea: Adapted from medical coherent fiber bundles with 10,000+ cores: a microLED array on the DRAM base die images straight into a bundle that lands on a photodiode array on the accelerator. The result is thousands of slow parallel lanes (~2 Gb/s each) with no lasers and no WDM.
why: Breaks interposer adjacency and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): HBM-class 2+ TB/s at ~1 pJ/bit over 1-10 m, so memory can live off-package in cheaper DDR-style dies.

title: Phone-filter piezo transducers send ultrasonic data vertically through stacks
idea: Adapted from AlN bulk-acoustic-wave filters in smartphones: thin piezo transducers on each die launch GHz acoustic pulses through the bonded silicon stack to receivers on other dies. Data TSVs are replaced by frequency- or time-multiplexed acoustic channels.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): could remove ~1-2k data TSVs per die and their keep-out zones, leaving only bonding and power vias.

title: Auto-parts remanufacturing for HBM: harvest, re-bump, redeploy stacks
idea: Adapted from the alternator/starter core-return model: HBM stacks from retired accelerators are thermally debonded, tested, re-bumped and mounted on CXL memory cards or low-cost interposers for inference and cache tiers.
why: Raises usable supply with no wafers: each retired 8-GPU node holds ~1-1.5 TB of HBM that is now shredded; reclaiming half adds supply at near-zero capital.

title: Car platform sharing: one DRAM core die, swappable interface chiplets
idea: Adapted from VW's shared MQB platform: fabs make one memory-array core die with a dense hybrid-bond face, and a separate interface chiplet turns it into DDR5, LPDDR, GDDR or HBM. Capacity moves between markets by changing only the cheap chiplet.
why: Capital and periphery (facts 4, 7): fewer mask sets, periphery moved to a cheaper logic node, and wafer starts reallocated in weeks, not quarters, during HBM/DDR shortages.

title: Repurpose LCD glass-panel lines to make giant memory interposers
idea: Adapted from display makers' Gen-8 (2.2 x 2.5 m) glass TFT lines with ~1.5 um lithography: pattern copper RDL and through-glass vias at panel scale. The panels become interposers that hold dozens of memory stacks around accelerators.
why: Silicon interposers are reticle-limited and capacity-bound; panels amortize over ~70x a 300 mm wafer's area, cutting interposer cost per area ~5-10x and freeing CoWoS capacity.

title: Space-solar Miura fold turns one thin DRAM sheet into a stack
idea: Adapted from Miura-ori folding of satellite solar arrays: a strip of DRAM dies is built on an ultra-thin flexible bonded film with continuous copper traces across the fold lines. The strip folds accordion-style into a 16-high stack whose wires wrap around the folds instead of passing through TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSVs, their keep-out and per-tier bonding steps, targeting ~20% lower stack cost and higher yield.

title: Fiber-drawing towers produce thousand-wire flexible memory ribbons
idea: Adapted from optical-fiber drawing: a macroscopic polymer preform embedded with copper rods is heated and drawn 100x thinner into kilometers of ribbon. Each ribbon holds thousands of insulated micro-wires at ~20 um pitch and links processor to memory away from the package.
why: Interposer area and adjacency limit: more DRAM can surround a processor through dense wide-slow buses at ~1 pJ/bit and very low cost per wire-meter.

title: Skyscraper sky lobbies: express TSV trunks plus local hops
idea: Adapted from tall-building elevator zoning: in a 24-32 high stack, a few wide 'express' TSV bundles run only to sky-lobby dies every 8 tiers. A thin repeater/switch layer there fans out to short local TSVs, so columns no longer pass through every die.
why: Enables taller stacks without TSV load growing on every tier: ~30-50% less TSV area per die, with pJ/bit held flat as stacks grow (fact 6).

title: Elevator destination dispatch: early row hints let DRAM pre-open
idea: Adapted from destination-dispatch elevators, where riders key in their floor in the lobby: cores send a cheap bank/row hint on a side channel tens of nanoseconds before the real request. The DRAM groups riders and opens each row once for many requests.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): ~20-40% less activation energy per useful bit and less row-hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: Aerospace time-triggered networks: compiler-scheduled DRAM with no command bus
idea: Adapted from time-triggered Ethernet and fly-by-wire scheduling: for static AI dataflow, the compiler emits a full timetable of activations and bursts and loads it into the DRAM base die. The die then streams on schedule, with no per-access commands, arbitration or handshakes.
why: Shrinks command/address pins and controller periphery (fact 7); bus efficiency rises from ~70% to >95%, roughly +30% bandwidth per pin.

title: Wireless-charger resonance recycles memory-bus switching energy
idea: Adapted from resonant inductive phone chargers: a wide HBM-style bus is driven as part of an LC tank with on-interposer spiral inductors. Line capacitance charges and discharges sinusoidally, and most of the CV^2 energy returns to the tank instead of being burned in drivers.
why: CV^2 floor and data movement (facts 5, 10): resonant drive can recover 50-80% of switching energy on wide, clock-like buses.

title: Data-center 48-volt distribution brought inside the memory stack
idea: Adapted from the 48 V rack transition: the HBM stack is fed at ~12 V through a few TSVs, and integrated switched-capacitor converters on each die step it down. This replaces hundreds of low-voltage power TSVs.
why: Power/ground take a large share of HBM TSVs and bumps; 10x less current frees ~30-50% of them for data or area and cuts IR-drop loss (fact 6).

title: Turbine-blade internal cooling channels inside HBM spacer layers
idea: Adapted from jet-engine blade cooling: serpentine microchannels are etched into thin silicon spacers placed every few dies and carry pumped dielectric coolant through the stack. Heat leaves from the stack interior instead of conducting up through 16 dies.
why: Thermal limits cap stack height and force 2x refresh above 85 C (fact 3); internal cooling could allow 24-32 high stacks and halve hot refresh.

title: MRI-style cryostat with superconducting interposer for memory links
idea: Adapted from the MRI magnet and superconducting-wire industry: the accelerator+DRAM module runs in a 77 K closed-cycle cryostat on an interposer with YBCO high-temperature superconducting traces. Links become nearly lossless, and DRAM leakage falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): near-zero resistive link loss and 100x+ retention at 77 K; this works only if cryocooler overhead stays below the energy saved.

title: Electricity spot market for rack-scale memory capacity and bandwidth
idea: Adapted from wholesale power markets with 5-minute nodal pricing: CXL-pooled memory in a cluster is auctioned in short intervals. Jobs bid for capacity and bandwidth, and lightly loaded servers sell their stranded DRAM back into the pool.
why: Raises usable supply by monetizing idle DRAM (typical utilization 40-60%); ~15-30% less DRAM purchased per cluster.

title: Film-editing proxies: fetch most-significant bit-planes first, refine on demand
idea: Adapted from VFX proxy editing and progressive JPEG: tensors are stored as bit-planes in separate DRAM rows. The accelerator fetches the top 4-8 bits first and requests lower planes only for values whose contribution matters (e.g., large attention scores).
why: Overfetch and data movement (facts 5, 8): ~30-60% fewer bits moved for inference at the same accuracy.

title: Stacked camera-sensor pixel bonding: per-subarray copper ports to logic
idea: Adapted from the pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonding of stacked smartphone image sensors: the DRAM array wafer bonds face-to-face to a logic wafer so each subarray (mat) has its own ~100-wire vertical port. Global I/O routing and shared periphery go away.
why: Periphery 49% of die (fact 7) and data movement: array efficiency toward ~75% and >10x bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical hops.

title: Cellphone LTCC radio modules become 30-layer ceramic memory substrates
idea: Adapted from the low-temperature co-fired ceramic tape lines of 1990s handset RF front-ends: silver wiring is screen-printed on 30+ green tape layers with punched vias and co-fired, then DRAM dies are flip-chipped around a processor. Dense routing comes with no silicon interposer and no lithography below 50 um.
why: Interposer cost and the CoWoS bottleneck: tape-casting and screen-printing tools are cheap and U.S.-buildable; 50 um lines support 512-1024-bit wide-slow buses per die at a fraction of interposer cost.

title: Infrared focal-plane cubes turned sideways: memory cube edge-bonds to processor
idea: Adapted from 1990s defense IR focal-plane cube stacking: thinned DRAM dies are laminated into a cube, one side face is lapped flat, and bond pads are patterned on that face with a contact aligner. The cube stands on edge so every die's edge talks straight down to the processor.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): zero TSVs, and each die gets its own direct edge bus; tier count is limited only by die thickness, using lapping and contact lithography.

title: Shingled solar-cell stacking: staircase DRAM dies with adhesive edge joints
idea: Adapted from shingled PV modules: DRAM dies are stacked offset like roof shingles so each die's pad row stays exposed, and each step is joined with dispensed electrically conductive adhesive instead of wire bonds or TSVs.
why: Low-capital stacking with no TSV etch or hybrid bonder, using 1990s dispensing robots; cost per stacked GB could fall 2-3x versus TSV HBM for capacity tiers.

title: RFID fluidic self-assembly drops memory dielets into interposer wells
idea: Adapted from 1990s fluidic self-assembly used by RFID tag makers: millions of small DRAM dielets suspended in liquid flow over an interposer with etched, shape-matched wells. The dielets settle into place by gravity and shape and are then bonded by reflow.
why: Small dielets yield far better (yield ~ e^-AD), and assembly runs massively in parallel, cutting pick-and-place cost and large-die yield loss.

title: Jacquard-loom woven wire interposer for memory buses
idea: Adapted from programmable textile looms: 15-25 um insulated copper wires are woven into a fabric of crossing warp and weft. Insulation is laser-stripped at programmed crossings and welded to form a custom X-Y routing grid, which is embedded in epoxy as the processor-memory substrate.
why: Replaces lithographic interposers with loom automation plus a laser; capital-light and U.S.-manufacturable, with thick copper giving low-loss long buses.

title: 1990s VCSEL ribbon optics disaggregate memory onto rack shelves
idea: Adapted from 1990s 12-channel 850 nm VCSEL parallel-optics datacom modules on multimode ribbon: memory moves to dedicated shelves linked to compute by many slow parallel VCSEL lanes, with driver and receiver chips at 180 nm or larger.
why: Raises usable supply through pooling and moves DRAM away from hot accelerators; mature GaAs VCSEL lines give ~5-10 pJ/bit at 2.5 Gb/s lanes, fine for capacity tiers.

title: Supermarket holographic scanners inspire free-space optical memory interconnect
idea: Adapted from the holographic optical elements in 1990s barcode scanners: a single cast hologram plate above the board redirects hundreds of VCSEL beams from memory packages to photodiodes on the processor, replacing board traces.
why: Board-level data movement and pin count: no copper trace loss, and routing is set by a cheap replicated hologram, so memory can be placed in 3D around the processor.

title: Transit-card inductive coupling powers and talks to glued stacks
idea: Adapted from contactless smart cards: each DRAM die gets on-die spiral coils in 180 nm-era metal, used both for near-field data links and for resonant power transfer like a card reader. The dies are simply glued together, with zero TSVs and zero bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): bad dies are swapped before gluing, and there is no via-related yield loss; no DRIE or hybrid bonding needed.

title: Nokia-era embedded-die circuit boards hide DRAM inside processor substrate
idea: Adapted from 1990s HDI cellphone boards with laser microvias and embedded components: thinned DRAM dies are laminated inside the processor's organic substrate directly under the SoC and connected by stacked laser microvias.
why: Memory wires shrink to ~1 mm with no silicon interposer or TSVs; ~3-5x lower pJ/bit than DDR using PCB-class tools found in U.S. shops.

title: Fax-machine run-length coding compresses sparse traffic on memory bus
idea: Adapted from Group 3 fax Modified Huffman/RLE: a 180 nm codec on the memory buffer encodes zero runs and repeated values in activations, sparse weights and KV-cache before they cross the bus and land in DRAM.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and effective capacity: ReLU and sparse tensors are often 50-90% zeros, so 2-5x fewer bits are moved and stored.

title: Telephone hybrid echo cancellation doubles bandwidth per memory pin
idea: Adapted from the 2-wire telephone hybrid and V.34/1000BASE-T echo cancellers: reads and writes travel on the same wire at the same moment, and each end subtracts its own transmitted signal using 180 nm analog circuits.
why: Pin and TSV count (facts 6, 7): 2x bandwidth per pin, or half the pins/TSVs for the same bandwidth, making up for slower old-node lanes.

title: Compact-disc scratch codes make TSV defects harmless
idea: Adapted from CD CIRC interleaving: each data word is spread across many TSVs with a Reed-Solomon erasure code, so a few open or leaky TSVs become erasures corrected on the fly instead of needing spare-TSV repair or scrapping the stack.
why: HBM yield down 20-30% (fact 6): could recover most TSV-related yield loss with ~10% extra wires and 180 nm codec logic.

title: Pupin loading coils make long interposer memory lines distortionless
idea: Adapted from the 1900 telephone loading coil: small thick-metal spiral inductors are added periodically along long memory traces to meet the Heaviside condition (L/C = R/G). A wide slow bus can then stretch 5-10 cm without equalizers.
why: More DRAM dies can sit around a processor (capacity) at near-HBM energy, and power-hungry equalization goes away.

title: Canal-lock stepwise charging lowers memory bus switching energy
idea: Adapted from canal locks that lift boats in stages: bus lines charge in sequence from a ladder of N tank capacitors at intermediate voltages instead of straight from VDD, so each transition dissipates ~1/N of the conventional CV^2.
why: CV^2 floor (fact 10): 4-step charging gives ~4x lower switching energy on wide slow buses, using only 180 nm switches and MIM or off-chip caps.

title: Power-line communication sends data over HBM power TSVs
idea: Adapted from home power-line networking: modulated high-frequency data is superimposed on the stack's many power/ground TSVs and planes through simple 180 nm couplers, so power vias also carry control, refresh and sideband traffic.
why: TSV count (fact 6): frees signal TSVs now spent on command and sideband, ~10-20% fewer TSVs, or more data lanes in the same footprint.

title: Railroad hump yard sorts memory requests on 180 nm buffer
idea: Adapted from gravity hump-yard classification: a 180 nm buffer chip between processor and DRAM bins incoming requests by bank and row onto 'classification tracks' with a deep sorting network. It then releases each 'train' as one activation followed by many column reads.
why: Overfetch and destructive read (fact 8): 2-3x higher row-hit rates on irregular workloads, cutting activation energy per useful bit and row-hammer pressure (fact 9).

title: MIDI-style memory: ship generator seeds, regenerate data beside DRAM
idea: Adapted from MIDI, which sends notes rather than audio: regenerable tensor parts (random projections, low-rank bases, positional tables) are stored as seeds plus generator code. A 180 nm PRNG/LFSR engine on the memory buffer recreates them on the fly instead of reading them.
why: Data movement and capacity: regenerable tensors are neither stored nor moved; ~10-30% capacity and bandwidth savings for suitable models.

title: Wartime auto-plant conversion: idle U.S. 200 mm fabs make interposers
idea: Adapted from Willow Run's conversion from cars to bombers: shuttered or underused U.S. 200 mm/180 nm fabs are retooled to make passive silicon interposers, RDL and DRIE TSVs, all of which need only 0.5-2 um features.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: packaging capacity in months at ~10% of new-fab cost, easing the CoWoS-class bottleneck that gates HBM.

title: Military fuzz-button connectors make solderless, reworkable memory stacks
idea: Adapted from fuzz-button (compressed gold-wire wad) interconnects in avionics: DRAM dies or packages stack in a clamped frame with fuzz-button arrays between them, so any failing die can be swapped after test with no reflow.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): one bad die no longer scraps a 12-16 die stack (~20-30% yield recovery), using 1990s machining and wire-forming tools.

title: Display-driver tape-automated bonding puts memory dies on reel-to-reel film
idea: Adapted from the chip-on-film/TAB lines that bonded 1990s LCD driver chips: DRAM dies are bonded with anisotropic conductive film onto polyimide tape patterned at 20-30 um pitch, reel-to-reel and solder-free at 150-200 C. The memory tapes then attach around the processor.
why: Avoids micro-bump and hybrid-bonding tool chokepoints; reel-to-reel throughput and cheap film carriers give wide modest-pitch buses at low capital.

title: Laptop heat pipes etched into silicon spacers cool tall stacks
idea: Adapted from laptop heat pipes: the 1994 Bosch DRIE process etches sealed micro heat-pipe channels with wicking grooves into silicon spacer dies inserted in the memory stack. Filled with water or methanol, they carry heat sideways to the lid passively.
why: Thermal limits on stack height and hot refresh (fact 3): ~2-5x lower stack thermal resistance, allowing taller stacks and halving high-temperature refresh.

title: Prestressed-concrete trick: stress films flatten ultra-thin memory stacks
idea: Adapted from prestressed concrete: calibrated PECVD nitride/oxide films are deposited on the back of each thinned DRAM die so their built-in stress cancels the warpage that appears at bonding temperature. 30 um dies then stack flat with simple thermocompression.
why: Warpage limits HBM yield and stack height (fact 6); targets both using 1990s deposition tools.

title: Congestion-charge pricing for DRAM row openings
idea: Adapted from London's congestion charge: the OS/hypervisor meters each process's row activations through memory-controller counters and charges them against a quota. Runtimes and allocators respond by restructuring data layouts for locality.
why: Overfetch and row hammer (facts 8, 9): ~20-40% fewer activations per useful bit and lower energy, with no new hardware or tools.
